This is a research-systems and science-education stance grounded in an address excerpt and editorial testimony.

name: Asiye Hatun
summary: Seventeenth-century Ottoman woman whose letters to her Halveti sheikh record dreams and waking visions during spiritual exercises; the corpus is a rare first-person record of a pre-Tanzimat woman and Sufi self-exploration.
lifespan: Active c.1641/42–1643/44; death described as second half of 17th century in UC Press reader; exact birth/death years not established.
perspective: The letters present dreams and waking visions as part of a disciple’s spiritual progress, with experiences organized around the sheikh’s guidance and stages of remembrance. A 2024 scholarly reading argues the work shifts traditional Sufi dream inquiry toward exploration of the individual inner self; that is an interpretation of her text, not a claim that she articulated this modern formulation.

readingPaths.title: Rüya Mektupları (Dream Letters)
readingPaths.yearLabel: Letters to Muslihuddin Efendi, c.1641/42–1643/44; modern transcription/translation editions include Cemal Kafadar (Oğlak, 1994) and The Ottoman World ch. 5
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the letters as spiritual progress reports: dreams and waking visions follow the sequence of Sufi remembrance (dhikr) and stages under her sheikh. This provides a firsthand record of devotional practice and self-exploration.
readingPaths.accessNote: The review page is open and reproduces a short verse excerpt, explains the editions, and points to the 1994 transcription and translated chapter. Full primary text was not opened in this review; the UC Press catalog confirms translated chapter attribution/translators but not its contents.

readingPaths.title: A Seventeenth-Century Sufi’s Self-Exploration: Asiye Hatun’s Rüya Mektupları
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the article’s abstract for its specific interpretive proposal: dream inquiry shifts from a traditional Sufi practice toward a form of inner-self exploration; it resists making gender alone determine the text’s meaning.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened bilingual abstract and article metadata; full text requires subscription and was not accessed.

readingPaths.title: Lamp for the Path to Enlightenment

name: Bhartṛhari
summary: The Vākyapadīya makes the analysis of grammar and language a philosophical inquiry into meaning, cognition, and reality; GRETIL preserves the Sanskrit text and opening verses.
lifespan: fl. c. 5th century CE; 450–510 is a scholarly estimate, not secure life dates.
perspective: Bhartṛhari models inquiry through close analysis of language: grammatical explanation can itself be a philosophical viewpoint (darśana), linking how words are understood with questions about reality and liberation. name: Charles Darwin
summary: In this autobiographical manuscript, Darwin recounts how his habits of observation, collection, and persistent attention shaped his scientific work. He describes keeping extensive notes and portfolios, testing ideas against contrary evidence, and revising or abandoning hypotheses when facts demanded it. He also reflects on the mental qualities and daily routines that supported his investigations, including methodical arrangement, patience in pondering unexplained problems, and the role of leisure and illness in his working life.
perspective: Reflects on his own mental development and working habits, emphasizing persistent attention, note-keeping, and willingness to discard hypotheses when evidence opposes them. Notes a gradual loss of aesthetic tastes alongside sustained interest in history, biography, and travel. Frames his scientific success as arising from steady love of science, industry in collecting facts, and patience in long reflection rather than exceptional quickness.

readingPaths.title: Recollections of the Development of My Mind and Character

name: Claude Bernard
summary: In this foundational work, Bernard examines how experimental reasoning operates in medicine and physiology. He distinguishes observation from experiment, stresses that experimentation is provoked observation, and argues that the investigator must doubt prior ideas, avoid fixed notions, and retain freedom of mind. He discusses induction, deduction, the experimental criterion, and proof and counterproof, presenting the experimental method as necessarily antisystematic and antidoctrinal. The work also reflects on scientific education, the laboratory as the place where methods are learned, and the necessity of balancing knowledge with original, creative thought.
perspective: Bernard describes experimental reasoning as grounded in doubt, verification, and the testing of hypotheses against observations. He contrasts the experimental spirit with systems and doctrines that resist revision, and warns against fixed ideas. He emphasizes that the investigator must remain free of philosophical or medical systems, learn methods in the laboratory, and preserve creative originality while acquiring knowledge. He also reflects on the emotional dimension of research, noting the persistent pull of the unknown alongside the satisfaction of discovery.

readingPaths.title: Introduction à l’étude de la médecine expérimentale
readingPaths.whyRead: For a classic account of experimental method, including observation, hypothesis, doubt, and verification in medicine and physiology.
readingPaths.accessNote: French original available via Project Gutenberg; English translations also exist.

summary: Discovered genetic and neurobiological causes of narcolepsy, including hypocretin/orexin signalling.
activity: Stanford profile lists current professorship, center directorship, research and publications; Stanford reported 2026 Lasker recognition.
perspective: Mignot describes crossing disciplinary boundaries, attending conferences outside his field for ideas, and making a risky bet on dog narcolepsy genetics despite skepticism.

readingPaths.title: A conversation with Emmanuel Mignot
readingPaths.whyRead: Mignot describes crossing disciplinary boundaries, attending conferences outside his field for ideas, and making a risky bet on dog narcolepsy genetics despite skepticism.
readingPaths.accessNote: Accessible institutional or journal interview text.

name: Emmanuel Saez
institution: University of California Berkeley; Director of the Stone Center on Wealth and Income Inequality
topics: connecting academic research to public debate
summary: The Piketty-Saez long-run top income share series built from administrative tax records - a named dataset that became the standard measurement infrastructure for inequality research and public debate - together with the sufficient-statistics approach to optimal income and capital taxation now standard in public finance
activity: Paper on California billionaire wealth revised August 2026; income-inequality data tables updated June 2026; current course listings Econ 131 Econ 230A Econ 2 and Econ 231
perspective: Saez advises beginning with a broad topic, examining the available data, and narrowing the question only then. The student interview makes this order of decisions explicit, rather than treating data as something found after a thesis is fixed.

readingPaths.title: Interview with Prof. Emmanuel Saez (Economics H195A)
readingPaths.whyRead: Saez explains his data-first method for choosing and narrowing a research question.
readingPaths.accessNote: Open web page hosted by UC Berkeley; interview conducted by Pooja Mehta for Prof. Martha Olney's seminar.

name: Emmanuelle Charpentier
summary: Discovery of tracrRNA and CRISPR-Cas9 mechanism enabling programmable genome editing
activity: Bio/patents/documentation current; crawled 2026
perspective: Charpentier frames science as detective work: curiosity and persistent questions guide it, and progress requires tolerating frustration while combining focused thought with collaboration.

readingPaths.title: Rencontre avec Emmanuelle Charpentier, prix Nobel de chimie
readingPaths.whyRead: First-person reflections on the emotional and collaborative texture of scientific inquiry.
readingPaths.accessNote: Accessible full text opened and read.

name: Emmy Noether
summary: Mathematician whose work helped establish abstract algebra and shaped modern mathematics.
perspective: In a contemporaneous memorial address, her student Pavel Alexandrov attributes to Noether a mathematical approach that seeks general formulations revealing a problem’s essential logical structure, and that moves from concrete mathematical substance toward general principles. He describes her as resisting symbol manipulation detached from reality.

readingPaths.title: Alexandrov on Emmy Noether (1935 memorial address)
readingPaths.whyRead: In a contemporaneous memorial address, her student Pavel Alexandrov attributes to Noether a mathematical approach that seeks general formulations revealing a problem’s essential logical structure, and that moves from concrete mathematical substance toward general principles. He describes her as resisting symbol manipulation detached from reality.
readingPaths.accessNote: A translated transcription of Alexandrov’s 1935 memorial address was inspected; attribution and context are given, but this is disciple testimony rather than Noether-authored prose.

name: Enheduanna
summary: Historical royal daughter of Sargon and high priestess at Ur; a corpus of hymns is attributed to her, with a five-century gap between life and extant school transmission made explicit in the scholarship.
lifespan: Old Akkadian period (often placed in the 23rd c. BCE; precise life dates unknown). Poems attributed to her were copied and studied in Old Babylonian schools about five centuries later.
perspective: In the attributed Exaltation, the speaker links hymn, lament, and a personal appeal after expulsion from ritual office, making devotional craft a way to narrate political dispossession and seek redress. The account is mediated by later manuscript copies and should not be treated as an unproblematic diary.

readingPaths.title: The Exaltation of Inana (Inana B)
readingPaths.yearLabel: Old Akkadian attributed; later Old Babylonian copies
readingPaths.whyRead: Read lines 66–154 for the first-person account of ritual service, exile, and the act of composing a hymn that asks for intervention.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened English translation/transliteration. This is a composite critical text; surviving copies postdate the attributed author by centuries.

name: Enrico Fermi
summary: Italian-American physicist whose work shaped quantum and nuclear physics; also wrote public explanations of contemporary physics.
perspective: Fermi explains difficult theory through experiments that distinguish competing mechanisms. In this short article he moves from ordinary phenomena to elementary events that can be made observable, then distinguishes what the evidence shows from the open question of whether atomic indeterminism is fundamental or reflects unobserved causes.

readingPaths.title: “Contemporary Problems of Physics” / “Problemi attuali della fisica”
readingPaths.yearLabel: 1929; Italian transcription and English translation published2023
readingPaths.whyRead: A short example of explaining theory through discriminating experiments and ending with a clearly stated unresolved question.
readingPaths.accessNote: Root read the English text and its historical introduction in Goldoni and Stefanini’s edition. The translators disclose some modernization of wording; Fermi’s possible motives are conjectures in their introduction, not his own statements.

name: Epeli Hauʻofa
summary: Hauʻofa’s essays, including “The Ocean in Us” and “Our Sea of Islands,” articulate a Pacific regional identity grounded in the shared ocean and challenge constricted framings of island peoples.
lifespan: 1939–2009; birth in Papua New Guinea to Tongan parents and academic career across the Pacific per UH Press author record. “The Ocean in Us” is a 1990s essay; this ANU Press chapter page is a later reprint, not the composition date.
perspective: Hauʻofa argues that a shared ocean can ground regional identity and rekindle ancestral mobility; his “sea of islands” framing counters representations of Pacific societies as isolated small islands. This is an explicit authored regional argument, not an inference from outsider ethnography.

readingPaths.title: “The Ocean in Us,” chapter 2
readingPaths.yearLabel: Essay from 1990s Hauʻofa writing, reprinted in a later ANU Press book; page does not show original composition date
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the author’s regional-identity argument and its relation to oceanic mobility; compare with “Our Sea of Islands” in the UH Press selected-work collection.
readingPaths.accessNote: ANU Press chapter page and opening argument inspected; not every chapter of We Are the Ocean was read.

name: Ephrem the Syrian (Ephraem of Syria)
summary: Ephrem composed Syriac hymns, poetic homilies and biblical commentaries; his works include hymns on Faith, Paradise, Nativity, the Church and controversies with other religious movements. Critical editions and translation histories differentiate authentic Syriac works from later works attributed to him in other languages.
lifespan: ca. 306–373 CE; birth/death dates approximate and locations vary across reference sources
perspective: His teaching practice makes poetry an instrument of communal learning: the hymns use parallel structures, imagery, wordplay and dramatic disputation to explore biblical and theological ideas, and historical accounts describe them as sung in Christian assemblies. The authentic Syriac corpus is better established than Greek and Latin materials transmitted under his name.

readingPaths.title: Nativity 17, Digital Syriac Corpus
readingPaths.yearLabel: Syriac hymn; base edition Edmund Beck, 1959
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the Syriac text in the encoded corpus alongside a translation identified in the Syriac editions guide; this provides a named text and original language rather than only a later attribution.
readingPaths.accessNote: Digital corpus page opened; Syriac text displayed, no English translation on that page. The corpus record identifies a critical base edition.

readingPaths.title: The Harp of the Spirit: 18 Poems of Saint Ephrem, trans. Sebastian Brock
readingPaths.whyRead: Use for carefully selected English translations; the opened bibliography guide identifies this as a recommended collection.
readingPaths.accessNote: Bibliographic route only; full book not open/read.

readingPaths.title: Ephraem of Syria, Encyclopedia of Religion entry
readingPaths.whyRead: For evidence on authentic corpus, teaching, communal hymn performance, and poetic form.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened full article.

name: Epictetus
summary: Reflective writing in practical philosophy.
perspective: The handbook associated with Epictetus repeatedly separates a person’s judgments and choices from outcomes they cannot command. It turns that distinction into exercises for responding to setbacks, ambition and other people.

readingPaths.title: Enchiridion — opening sections
readingPaths.whyRead: Start with the opening distinctions, then examine the proposed exercises critically against your own experience.
readingPaths.accessNote: Disciple Arrian compiled the handbook from Epictetus’s teaching; it is not an autograph memoir. English translation hosted by MIT.

name: Eric Betzig
institution: Howard Hughes Medical Institute; Janelia Research Campus; University of California, Berkeley
summary: Developed super-resolution fluorescence microscopy and successive imaging platforms that resolve and track structures in living cells
activity: Janelia page identifies Betzig as Senior Fellow and HHMI investigator and describes current imaging work; HHMI profile crawled 2026-06-20 and Janelia page 2026-09-13
perspective: Betzig values collisions between disciplines and describes a willingness to leave a successful line of work to create risky new directions.

readingPaths.title: Faculty recruit: Betzig (transcript)
readingPaths.whyRead: A direct interview on cross-disciplinary work and the personal appetite for risky scientific directions.
readingPaths.accessNote: Accessible full text opened and read.

name: Eric Cornell

summary: Creation and study of Bose-Einstein condensates in dilute atomic gases and later precision tests using ultracold matter
activity: CU Boulder profile gives current research interests and group publications; 2026 NASA taskbook lists Cornell as active PI; audited 2026-09-20
perspective: Cornell describes research as needing both close focus and periodic perspective shifts to reassess what matters; he also reflects on collaboration as a source of joy and research-career insecurity.

readingPaths.title: Imposter Syndrome, the Joys of Physics, and What Makes a Good Researcher
readingPaths.whyRead: Cornell describes research as needing both close focus and periodic perspective shifts to reassess what matters; he also reflects on collaboration as a source of joy and research-career insecurity.
readingPaths.accessNote: Accessible institutional or journal interview text.

name: Eric F. Wieschaus
institution: Princeton University; Lewis-Sigler Institute for Integrative Genomics; HHMI
topics: life design for daily lab access
summary: Mapped the genetic toolkit controlling early Drosophila embryonic development and showed its deep conservation across animals, transforming developmental biology.
activity: Wieschaus Lab was crawled last month with current people and recent publications; Princeton profile was crawled yesterday and lists current senior scholar/emeritus role and ongoing research.
perspective: Sustains a scientist's life by resisting status-driven distraction, staying personally at the bench, choosing doable hard questions, and keeping research scaled to hands-on collaboration.

readingPaths.title: Eric F. Wieschaus – Interview
readingPaths.whyRead: First-person reflections on lab life, ambition, collaboration, and deliberate choices after the Nobel Prize.
readingPaths.accessNote: Page includes embedded video and full transcript.

name: Eric Hoffer
summary: Self-educated philosopher and essayist whose writing drew on work and observation outside academic institutions.
perspective: The Hoover archive reconstructs a concrete writing practice from Hoffer’s letters and notebooks: he worked out thoughts on regular walks, wrote them down afterward, and revisited notebook material for later books. It also traces his initial resistance to autobiography and his later reuse of early fiction in Truth Imagined; this is archival synthesis, not a first-person reading of the memoir.

readingPaths.title: Truth Imagined
readingPaths.whyRead: Read Hoffer’s memoir alongside the Hoover account of his notebooks and writing process to see how he narrates lived experience and early work.
readingPaths.accessNote: Google Books identifies the memoir and exposes section contents and limited preview; the full book was not read.

readingPaths.title: The Longshoreman Philosopher
readingPaths.whyRead: The archive article discusses Hoffer’s letters, 130-plus notebooks, daily walk-and-note practice, revision, and reuse of early fiction in his memoir.
readingPaths.accessNote: Full Hoover Institution article opened; it is an archivist’s account of manuscript and letter evidence, not Hoffer’s own text.

name: Eric Kandel
institution: Columbia University; Kavli Institute for Brain Science; HHMI
summary: Linked cellular and molecular changes in neurons to learning and memory, using Aplysia and vertebrate models to establish mechanisms of short- and long-term memory.
activity: Columbia profile was crawled today and lists current emeritus and Kavli/HHMI roles, research interests, selected publications, and textbook leadership; Lasker provides independent consensus recognition.
perspective: Kandel emphasizes choosing the experimental organism and preparation that make a question answerable, then using reduction to clarify complex biological mechanisms.

readingPaths.title: Interview with Eric Kandel
readingPaths.whyRead: A reflective account of the experimental strategy behind his neuroscience, not only a summary of results.
readingPaths.accessNote: Accessible full text opened and read.

name: Ernst Friedrich Schumacher
summary: Economist whose development and technology writing argued for economic scale and methods fitted to human and ecological needs.
perspective: Schumacher makes economic reasoning answerable to prior judgments about right livelihood and human purpose instead of presenting it as value-free. Historical scholarship connects this perspective to his advisory experience in Burma; his essay is useful as a concrete example of how an ethical framework changes what counts as economic success.

readingPaths.title: “Buddhist Economics”
readingPaths.yearLabel: First published 1966; included in Small Is Beautiful (1973)
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the essay’s opening as a short demonstration of how a different ethical premise changes economic questions and definitions.
readingPaths.accessNote: Full essay available online; interpretation is grounded in its opening and source history.

name: Ernst Mach
summary: Advanced experimental research on acoustics, shock waves, and perception, and developed influential empiricist critiques of scientific concepts and mechanics.
perspective: Mach treats inquiry as a psychological and epistemic activity, attending to how knowledge is organized and revised.

readingPaths.title: Popular Scientific Lectures — preface and inquiry-focused lectures
readingPaths.yearLabel: English third revised and enlarged edition, 1898; translated by Thomas J. McCormack
readingPaths.whyRead: Start with Mach’s preface, then “On the Economical Nature of Physical Inquiry,” “On Transformation and Adaptation in Scientific Thought,” and “On the Part Played by Accident in Invention and Discovery.” These sections give his own account of how scientific ideas should be selected, communicated and developed.
readingPaths.accessNote: Project Gutenberg full text opened; preface and contents inspected. English translation by T. J. McCormack; the third revised/enlarged edition is dated 1898. This is an additive entry point, not a replacement of Knowledge and Error.

name: Erwin Chargaff
summary: Biochemist whose work helped establish key empirical regularities in DNA composition.
perspective: In Heraclitean Fire, Chargaff asks what science is and how it is practiced, describing science as a search for truth about nature and lamenting its separation from philosophy and its bureaucratic professionalization. This is first-person material from the memoir, not an editorial paraphrase.

readingPaths.title: Heraclitean Fire: Sketches from a Life Before Nature
readingPaths.whyRead: Chargaff reflects directly on science’s purpose, the nature of discovery, his own professional dissatisfaction, and the link between science and philosophy.
readingPaths.accessNote: Full primary text opened in a digitized reader; chapters and first-person reflections inspected.

name: Erwin Neher
institution: Max Planck Institute for Multidisciplinary Sciences; University of Göttingen, emeritus
summary: Co-developed the patch-clamp technique and used it to establish how single ion channels generate cellular electrical signals.
activity: Max Planck emeritus profile was crawled 6 days ago with current contact, title, and institutional affiliation; MPG profile records patch-clamp contribution.
perspective: Neher describes how failed experiments and frustration can prompt a new angle, changed conditions, or a different experiment; he also recounts deliberate topic choice across biophysics and collaboration.

readingPaths.title: Interview Erwin Neher
readingPaths.whyRead: Neher describes how failed experiments and frustration can prompt a new angle, changed conditions, or a different experiment; he also recounts deliberate topic choice across biophysics and collaboration.
readingPaths.accessNote: Accessible institutional or journal interview text.

name: Erwin Schrödinger
summary: Formulated wave mechanics and the Schrödinger equation, a central mathematical formulation of quantum theory; also wrote on biology and philosophy.
perspective: Schrödinger’s chapter reflects on the relation between scientific description and the observer’s wider worldview, showing that he saw scientific models as partial accounts.

readingPaths.title: My View of the World: “Metaphysics in General”
readingPaths.whyRead: An accessible chapter on the limits and standpoint of scientific description.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened source supports this title/description; not represented as a complete reading of the work.

name: Esther Duflo
institution: MIT; University of Zurich; Collège de France; J-PAL
summary: Evidence-based development economics using randomized evaluations and policy experiments
activity: MIT page has current affiliations, publications, books, CV, and copyright 2026
perspective: Duflo describes experiments as a way to identify causal effects within the context where they were run, while rejecting criticism that merely restates the need for good design. Her framing stresses the interplay of theory and empirical observation rather than treating randomization as a universal answer.

readingPaths.title: Interview with Esther Duflo
readingPaths.whyRead: A direct discussion of experimental research’s strengths and limitations, including why context matters and how to reason about well-run studies.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened interview text; synthesis limited to the displayed Q&A.

name: Evelyn Fox Keller
summary: Physicist, mathematical biologist and historian/philosopher of science known for work on gender, language and scientific objectivity.
perspective: Keller’s own interdisciplinary work, as described by MIT, examines how values, gendered assumptions and metaphors shape scientific hypotheses and the ideal of objective inquiry. Her account of Barbara McClintock’s research methods helped challenge narrow definitions of discovery while avoiding the claim that a research style is intrinsically feminine.

readingPaths.title: Reflections on Gender and Science
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the book’s opening essays for her analysis of objectivity and how scientific institutions define legitimate styles of thought.
readingPaths.accessNote: Yale bibliographic page and MIT editorial retrospective inspected; publisher description PDF failed; full book not read.

name: Ewine van Dishoeck
institution: Leiden University, emerita; Leiden Observatory
summary: Combined observational, theoretical, and laboratory astrochemistry to explain molecular clouds and star and planet formation.
activity: Leiden profile is reachable and current; links her research interests and personal homepage.
perspective: Van Dishoeck emphasizes that research careers rarely follow a plan and that unexpected opportunities need to be taken. In inquiry, she directs attention toward weak spectral features because overlooked signals may open a new line of work; she also describes long time scales and responsibility to build for future researchers.

readingPaths.title: Ewine van Dishoeck on the art of making a career
readingPaths.whyRead: A practical account of how unexpected opportunities redirected her from theoretical chemistry to astrochemistry and of how weak spectral features can lead to new questions.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened full university magazine interview.

name: F. Duncan M. Haldane
summary: Topological phases of matter; Haldane model; quantum Hall and spin-chain theory
activity: Current personal Princeton scholar page states ongoing research and links current research interests
perspective: Haldane describes learning to simplify a problem into a toy model that exposes its essential physics, a practice shaped by mentors and by movement across research environments.

readingPaths.title: Interview with Duncan Haldane
readingPaths.whyRead: A first-person account of how mentorship and simplification shape his research practice.
readingPaths.accessNote: Accessible full text opened and read.

name: Fei Xiaotong
summary: Anthropologist and sociologist whose studies of Chinese rural communities shaped modern Chinese sociology.
perspective: From the Soil develops social theory from fieldwork and a cross-cultural position: the publisher notes that Fei wrote for Chinese readers from a Chinese point of view after fieldwork at home and residence in the West. His plain, comparative style connects social organization to everyday moral relations.

readingPaths.title: From the Soil
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the short chapters on rural social organization and compare the translator’s account of how Fei grounded theory in fieldwork.
readingPaths.accessNote: Publisher’s detailed description and contents inspected; full English edition not read.

name: Fei-Fei Li
institution: Stanford University, Sequoia Professor; Stanford HAI co-director; World Labs
summary: Created ImageNet and large-scale visual recognition benchmarks that helped establish modern data-driven computer vision and deep learning.
activity: Stanford profile currently lists her professorship, HAI leadership, World Labs role and 2026-27 teaching/research activity.
perspective: Li describes research as a process sustained by curiosity and freedom, while accepting uncertainty and failure as part of trying ambitious ideas.

readingPaths.title: Interview with Fei-Fei Li
readingPaths.whyRead: First-person reflections on the lived process of research and tolerance for uncertainty.
readingPaths.accessNote: Accessible full text opened and read.

name: Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala
summary: Indigenous Andean author and artist of a 1,200-page illustrated chronicle addressed to Philip III.
perspective: The chronicle combines an author’s account of Andean/colonial life with a reform proposal; the Royal Danish Library describes his use of 398 drawings as an integral, persuasive medium.

readingPaths.title: El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno
readingPaths.whyRead: Explore the facsimile and transcription as a visual-textual argument addressed to the Spanish king.
readingPaths.accessNote: Royal Danish Library digital autograph facsimile with scholarly editor Rolena Adorno; Spanish with Quechua passages.

readingPaths.title: El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the manuscript’s opening and reform address to see an Andean history joined to a direct argument about colonial governance.
readingPaths.accessNote: Royal Danish Library item page describes the complete digitized manuscript and links to the viewer; the viewer returned 403 in this verification pass, so access to the facsimile itself was not confirmed. The work is in Spanish and Quechua; its authored status and contents are supported by the Library and UNESCO nomination.

readingPaths.title: UNESCO Memory of the World nomination: Nueva corónica
readingPaths.whyRead: Use for scholarly/archival context on the manuscript’s authorship, purpose, and Andean perspective.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened institutional nomination PDF describing the work; secondary description, not the primary manuscript.

name: Fernando de Alva Ixtlilxochitl

readingPaths.title: History of the Chichimeca Nation
readingPaths.yearLabel: 2019 English translation/edition; original compilation late 16th–first half 17th c.
readingPaths.whyRead: Consult the chronicle through the 2019 critical translation and its introduction on Indigenous sources, source comparison, and Nahua political history.
readingPaths.accessNote: Publisher description opened; full text not read. Scholarly editors identify original author manuscript in Códice Chimalpahin, vol. 2.

readingPaths.title: Yukitaka Inoue Okubo review, Estudios de Cultura Náhuatl / UNAM
readingPaths.whyRead: Read for title/date/manuscript cautions and the basis of the modern edition.

name: Finn E. Kydland
institution: University of California, Santa Barbara; Carnegie Mellon University; Norwegian School of Economics

activity: UCSB profile was crawled yesterday and lists current professorships, affiliations, and Nobel-linked research description.

readingPaths.title: A Conversation with Finn Kydland
readingPaths.whyRead: A substantial first-person account of research assumptions, modeling choices and what inquiry should explore.
readingPaths.accessNote: Accessible full text opened and read.

readingPaths.title: Novum Organum — preface and Book I

name: Francis Harry Compton Crick
summary: Molecular biologist who, with James Watson, proposed the double-helical structure of DNA and later studied the genetic code and consciousness.

readingPaths.title: What Mad Pursuit: A Personal View of Scientific Discovery
readingPaths.whyRead: Use the memoir’s account of theory formation and problem choice; Sidney Altman’s review identifies its specific discussion of Crick’s developing method and uncertainty in biological theory.

name: Frank Wilczek
institution: Massachusetts Institute of Technology; Arizona State University
summary: Asymptotic freedom in the strong interaction and wide-ranging theoretical work connecting fundamental laws, matter, and cosmology
activity: Personal site has About, research themes, books, lectures, and current ASU-linked material; crawled 6 days ago; audited 2026-09-20
perspective: Wilczek describes basic research as long-term, curiosity-driven entry into the unknown, with practical innovation often following from discoveries made without that immediate aim.

readingPaths.whyRead: A first-person account of why basic research matters and how it relates to philosophy and innovation.
readingPaths.accessNote: Accessible full text opened and read.

name: Frantz Fanon
summary: Martinican-born psychiatrist and anticolonial writer whose political essays and letters traced colonialism and liberation.
perspective: In his resignation letter, Fanon examines when persistence in professional work becomes self-deception. He concludes that he cannot practice humane psychiatry inside a social order he believes systematically defeats its purpose.

readingPaths.title: Letter of resignation to the Resident Minister
readingPaths.whyRead: A concrete account of professional conscience: deciding when remaining inside an institution contradicts the purpose of one’s work.
readingPaths.accessNote: Original French letter excerpt read in a published history textbook. The page also contains teaching exercises; the letter itself is clearly delimited. The wider collection is Toward the African Revolution.

name: François Jacob
summary: Reflective writing in biology.
perspective: Jacob connects scientific formation to childhood, war and the unfamiliar social habits of a new research community. The autobiography asks how these different experiences became parts of one working life.

readingPaths.title: The Statue Within: An Autobiography
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the memoir and the CSHL edition’s preface for his account of entering research and encountering informal American science.
readingPaths.accessNote: Publisher-supplied description on Google Books checked; full memoir not reviewed.

name: Françoise Barré-Sinoussi

readingPaths.title: Françoise Barré-Sinoussi’s Souvenir Album – Interview
readingPaths.yearLabel: 2023 Institut Pasteur press kit, interview section

readingPaths.title: Home Is Where the Wind Blows: Chapters from a Cosmologist’s Life
readingPaths.whyRead: The publisher frames the memoir around challenging established thinking, doing science, and working through major questions.

name: Frederick Douglass

name: Gaius Musonius Rufus

perspective: In the preserved lecture on women’s education, Musonius argues from shared human reason and capacity for virtue to equal access to philosophical training, then tests philosophy by whether it changes conduct. He makes the practical effects of study the criterion, while the surviving speech is mediated through later testimony and not securely an autograph work.

readingPaths.yearLabel: First-century teaching preserved in later testimony; exact composition/transmission date uncertain
readingPaths.whyRead: Read sections 1–7 for his reasoning from shared rational capacity to women’s education, and for his insistence that philosophical argument must translate into virtuous practice. Compare with the critical-edition listing for Cora Lutz’s translation.

name: George A. Akerlof
institution: Georgetown University, Professor Emeritus; University of California, Berkeley, emeritus

perspective: Akerlof treats economics as a serious, history-inflected and policy-relevant inquiry, deliberately resisting the solemn certainties of the official competitive general equilibrium model. He prizes an outsider's identity and curiosity over inherited family expectations, and uses richer mathematical structures, like fibre bundles rather than clear surfaces, to capture economic reality. His instinct is to seek theories serious yet less solemn, tied to concrete unemployment and social questions rather than formal elegance alone.

readingPaths.title: George A. Akerlof – Biographical

name: Giambattista Vico
summary: Neapolitan professor of rhetoric and philosopher whose Scienza nuova advanced a method combining philosophical principles with philological evidence to understand human-made institutions; his educational oration argues for balancing analytic critique with ars topica.

perspective: In De nostri temporis studiorum ratione, Vico grants modern critique and analytic geometry real powers but argues that exclusive emphasis on them weakens imagination, memory, eloquence, and practical learning. In the New Science he links knowledge of human affairs to tracing how people made them and joins philosophical principles to philological evidence.

readingPaths.title: On the Study Methods of Our Time (De nostri temporis studiorum ratione)
readingPaths.yearLabel: Oration delivered 1708; expanded and published 1709; extant transcription source is Opera latina I (Milan, 1835)

readingPaths.whyRead: NYU/Columbia Libraries' Arabic Collections Online record provides the 1893/94 Cairo Arabic edition and direct PDF downloads. MIT Libraries' opened guide describes the Muqaddima as including discussion of the process of writing history and links the full-text Arabic edition.
readingPaths.accessNote: NYU/Columbia digitized Arabic edition and MIT Libraries English guide inspected. The Arabic facsimile is not an English translation; no complete reading is claimed.

aliases: Abū Zayd ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Khaldūn

name: Ibn Miskawayh
summary: Author of Tahdhīb al-Akhlāq (Refinement of Character) and Tajarib al-Umam (Experiences of the Nations).
lifespan: 932–1030 (death); birth date given as 932 by Oxford Handbook; confirm if imported
perspective: The accessible scholarly account reports that Miskawayh begins Tahdhīb al-Akhlāq with an account of the soul; his text can be approached as moral training grounded in psychological analysis rather than a list of detached rules.

readingPaths.title: Tahdhīb al-akhlāq wa-taṭhīr al-aʿrāq (Refinement of Character)
readingPaths.whyRead: Use the opening discussion of the soul and the later account of habituation/virtue as a route into Miskawayh’s ethical psychology; compare with the scholarly chapter and Oxford treatment of his virtue ethics.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened the digitized Arabic edition’s catalog record and PDF controls; no PDF pages read. Library/public-domain scan route; interpretive description is based on opened scholarly chapter.

aliases: Abū ʿAlī Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb Miskawayh

name: Ibn Rushd (Averroes)
summary: Andalusian philosopher and jurist whose Decisive Treatise addresses the relation between philosophical inquiry and religious law.
perspective: The Decisive Treatise makes a case for philosophical reflection as a disciplined inquiry into beings and considers who is authorized to undertake it. The useful perspective is an argument about the conditions and obligations of inquiry rather than a personal memoir.

readingPaths.title: The Decisive Treatise
readingPaths.whyRead: A direct argument for reflective inquiry and the conditions under which philosophy should be practiced.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened English translation PDF; contextualized by Yale and Stanford reference pages.

aliases: Abū al-Walīd Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad Ibn Rushd

name: Ibn Sina
country: Bukhara and Iranian lands / Central and West Asia
summary: A major philosopher and physician whose systematic works shaped Islamic philosophy and medieval Latin scholasticism.
perspective: In the autobiography dictated to his disciple al-Jūzjānī, Avicenna’s intellectual formation is presented as a combination of ordered study and independent verification or intuition. A difficult text may require another scholar’s explanation; when a problem resists solution, the account describes persistence and seeking inspiration. Scholars caution that the autobiography is stylized and philosophically programmatic, so this is an attributed intellectual model rather than an unmediated diary.

readingPaths.title: Autobiography (Sargodhašt), in W. E. Gohlman, The Life of Ibn Sina
readingPaths.whyRead: The article gives provenance and identifies Gohlman’s critical edition with facing English translation. It also explains how the autobiography uses study and intuition as an epistemological model.
readingPaths.accessNote: The autobiography was not directly opened; the source is a substantive scholarly analysis and bibliographic route. The continuation of the biography is by disciple al-Jūzjānī, and the account is stylized.

aliases: Abū ʿAlī al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sīnā

name: Ibn Ṭufayl
summary: Andalusi philosopher and author of the surviving philosophical fable Hayy ibn Yaqzan.
lifespan: d. 1185; birth date not established here
perspective: The University of Chicago edition describes Hayy’s discoveries about nature, God and human place as developing without society, language or tradition; the story tests the scope of unaided learning and the difference between individual understanding and public life.

readingPaths.title: Hayy ibn Yaqzan: A Philosophical Tale
readingPaths.yearLabel: 12th c.; composition commonly placed c. 1177–1182, but exact dates are debated
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the philosophical narrative with Lenn Goodman’s translation commentary; follow the islander’s stages of observation, inference and encounter with society.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened scholarly publisher page and summary, not the translation itself; translation, introduction and notes are available through library/purchase.

aliases: Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Ṭufayl

name: Ida West
summary: Palawa/Tasmanian Aboriginal elder and writer whose 1984 memoir records her life, advocacy, and experience of community and public service.
lifespan: 1919–2003; Pride Against Prejudice published 1984.
perspective: In the memoir preface, West objects to generations of European authors speaking about Aboriginal people and using stigmatizing labels; she presents her own account as a way to reclaim Indigenous self-description. This is a short excerpt, so fuller characterization requires reading the memoir.

readingPaths.title: Pride Against Prejudice: Reminiscences of a Tasmanian Aborigine
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the preface passage on outsider authorship and naming, then the memoir for the wider community account.
readingPaths.accessNote: Libraries Tasmania opened and quotes the preface; full memoir was not accessed.

readingPaths.title: Aunty Ida West AM, Libraries Tasmania
readingPaths.whyRead: Use for identity, dates, roles, and publication details.
readingPaths.accessNote: Full page opened; identity and publication details inspected.

name: Inca Garcilaso de la Vega
summary: Peruvian-born mestizo chronicler who interpreted Inca and Spanish histories for readers in Spain and the Americas; his work is a major early modern account of Andean memory and colonial encounter.
lifespan: 1539–1616; Comentarios reales published 1609; the 1617 second part was published posthumously.
perspective: In the preface to Comentarios reales, he argues Spanish writers have given incomplete accounts of Peru and invokes his Cuzco birth, bilingual inheritance, and natural love of patria as grounds for correcting them. This is an authorial claim and a self-positioned historical method, not a guarantee of neutral representation.

readingPaths.title: Comentarios reales de los Incas, first part, prologue
readingPaths.whyRead: The prologue states how he selects and weighs oral and written testimony and why he preserves foundational Andean traditions. Read alongside scholarship on its bilingual and bicultural setting.
readingPaths.accessNote: Inspected a Spanish text scan and a University of Navarra dissertation abstract describing its critical edition; no English translation used.

readingPaths.title: Comentarios reales de los Incas
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the authorial preface for his argument about Spanish accounts, native knowledge, and patriotic motive; consult the opening chapters for his first-person Cuzco context.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened RAE digitized PDF and inspected the preface and selected passages; not the full volume.

readingPaths.title: “Noble Lady” / “Sumaq Ñusta,” Stanford Global Medieval Sourcebook
readingPaths.whyRead: Read as a separate Quechua lyric route with notes on textual transmission and edition history.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened Stanford source page and its editorial apparatus; excerpt is separate from the preface argument.

El Inca Garcilaso de la Vega

name: Ingrid Daubechies
institution: Duke University, emerita
summary: Developed wavelet theory and mathematical tools that became standard across signal processing, imaging, data analysis, and applied science.
activity: Duke Scholars profile has current honors, grants and emerita affiliation through 2026; NSF profile corroborates.
perspective: Daubechies treats mathematics as a human construction and emphasizes that applied and pure work can feel alike; precise reasoning and pattern-building are shared capacities rather than an inaccessible innate gift.

readingPaths.title: An interview with Ingrid Daubechies
readingPaths.whyRead: A long first-person conversation on the character of mathematical work and on inclusion in the profession.
readingPaths.accessNote: Accessible full text opened and read.

name: Isaac Newton
summary: Newton’s optics program combines controlled experiment and mathematical analysis; the queries frame unresolved phenomena as further questions for investigation.
lifespan: 1642–1727 (Old Style birth 1642; New Style 1643)
perspective: In Opticks Query 31, Newton treats “attraction” as a provisional name for observed tendencies rather than a settled account of their cause. He advises first determining from phenomena which bodies attract and the laws of those tendencies, then investigating causes.

readingPaths.title: Opticks, Query 31
readingPaths.yearLabel: 1718 edition of the Third Book of Opticks
readingPaths.whyRead: Query 31 asks whether attractive forces explain reflection, refraction, inflexion and related phenomena, then treats “attraction” as a provisional name rather than a settled cause. Newton recommends first learning from phenomena which bodies attract and the laws of attraction, then asking about the cause. This gives a direct case for separating empirical regularities from causal explanation.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened the Newton Project normalized transcription; read Query 31 only. The page identifies its source as the 1718 second edition and notes silent editorial regularization.

name: Isabella M. Weber
institution: University of Massachusetts Amherst, Associate Professor of Economics
summary: Historical work on China and contemporary work on administered prices and inflation policy reshaped debates on market transition and price controls.
activity: UMass profile lists current appointment, publications, honors, and active research; accessed 2026-09-20
perspective: Weber describes studying reform through experimentation at the margins: attend to actual outcomes, systematize what succeeds, and generalize gradually while preserving system stability rather than imposing a complete blueprint.

readingPaths.title: China’s Economic Reforms: An Interview with Isabella Weber
readingPaths.whyRead: First-person interview lays out an inductive, experimental approach to institutional change.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened and inspected; this packet summarizes the interview/lecture text, not a full-book claim.

name: Isabelle Stengers
summary: Philosopher of science whose work examines scientific practice, public engagement and the politics of knowledge.
lifespan: 1949–None
perspective: Her account of “slow science” treats research as socially entangled and ethically answerable: disclose the limits of claims, allow failure and uncertainty to be discussed, and engage publics without using expertise to silence them.

readingPaths.title: Another Science is Possible: A Manifesto for Slow Science
readingPaths.whyRead: Use this short manifesto to examine her account of pacing, failure and public responsibility in research.
readingPaths.accessNote: Official publisher description inspected; sample chapter link returned 403, so the book itself was not read.

name: Italo Calvino
summary: Italian novelist and essayist who prepared the Charles Eliot Norton lectures on literary values for the next millennium.
perspective: Calvino turns qualities he values in writing—lightness, quickness, exactitude, visibility and multiplicity—into an explicit account of literary practice. These are five completed lectures; the planned sixth, on consistency, was not written.

readingPaths.title: Six Memos for the Next Millennium
readingPaths.yearLabel: Prepared 1985; posthumous book 1988; Patrick Creagh translation
readingPaths.whyRead: A writer examines which qualities his craft should preserve, organizing the discussion around five different demands on a piece of writing.
readingPaths.accessNote: Publisher-supplied Google Books description and contents checked, alongside Calvino’s introductory excerpt at Siruela. Five lectures were completed; none delivered. Full lectures not read.

name: Ivan E. Sutherland
institution: Asynchronous Research Center; Portland State University; Visiting Scientist and Co-Founder
primary: Asynchronous and self-timed digital system design
topics: Asynchronous and self-timed digital system design
summary: Founded the modern self-timed circuit research programme with Micropipelines (1989 Turing Award Lecture); co-developed the Logical Effort method for CMOS delay estimation now standard in VLSI teaching and practice; founded and headed the Caltech Computer Science Department 1976-1980 during the Mead-Conway VLSI revolution; co-founded the Asynchronous Research Center in 2008
activity: Homepage carries a 2026 copyright and names him as co-founder with his CV dated October 2024; the people page serves a February 2026 team photograph; teaching page lists Superconducting Digital Circuits taught Fall 2024 with him as an instructor; publications list a 2024 Micropipelines United paper and two 2023 IEEE Transactions on Applied Superconductivity papers with him as author
perspective: Sutherland reflects on a failed networking initiative and the lesson that an idea and funding alone do not create research momentum; he contrasts that experience with the value of a clear, focused goal pursued through multiple possible approaches.

readingPaths.title: Oral History of Ivan Sutherland, Part 1
readingPaths.whyRead: Sutherland reflects on a failed networking initiative and the lesson that an idea and funding alone do not create research momentum; he contrasts that experience with the value of a clear, focused goal pursued through multiple possible approaches.
readingPaths.accessNote: Accessible primary or institutional interview/memoir text.

name: Ivan Illich
summary: A social critic whose work examined how institutional systems and technologies shape human autonomy.
perspective: Illich expands “tool” to include institutions and systems that produce education, health, knowledge and decisions. This lets him ask when designed means remain under people’s control and when the surrounding society is reorganized around them.

readingPaths.title: Tools for Conviviality, “Conviviality” excerpt
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the chapter excerpt for Illich’s expansive definition of tools and his question of how they affect autonomy.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened an excerpt from the book and read Illich’s definition of “tool”; not represented as a complete reading of the book.

name: J. B. S. Haldane
summary: Biologist and geneticist whose work helped establish population genetics and whose public writing connected science to ordinary life and politics.
perspective: Haldane describes learning science through apprenticeship rather than through his formal classical degree, then treats public explanation as a scientist’s responsibility. His own note also places scientific work inside political and wartime circumstances rather than presenting research as detached from life.

readingPaths.title: Autobiographical Notes circa 1940
readingPaths.whyRead: Haldane gives a direct account of how apprenticeship shaped his scientific education and argues that scientists should make science intelligible to ordinary readers.
readingPaths.accessNote: The page provides a transcription of Haldane’s first-person notes and identifies them as circa 1940; the UCL archive independently documents the collection and his scientific career.

name: J. C. Kumarappa
summary: Economist and rural development practitioner who combined public-finance analysis with village surveys and work on village industries.
lifespan: born 1892; death year not verified in an accessible opened source
perspective: In Economy of Permanence, written partly in jail, Kumarappa derives a social account of work from observation of interdependence in nature. He treats scientific study as learning how systems function, then asks how human work can avoid violence and serve a wider community. A biographical account of his training documents how debate over profit-centered economics prompted him to revise his assumptions and test ideas through rural surveys.

readingPaths.title: Economy of Permanence: A quest for a social order based on non-violence
readingPaths.whyRead: Kumarappa develops an ecological account of work and cooperation, explains his approach in a signed preface and wrote the first part while imprisoned. The book joins observations about nature to a practical theory of economics.
readingPaths.accessNote: Full primary book accessible online; Gandhi’s foreword is separate from Kumarappa’s signed preface and text.

name: J. D. Bernal
summary: Scientist and historian of science whose work connected research with social organization and policy.
perspective: In The Social Function of Science Bernal argues that science has social purposes and that scientific methods must expand beyond repetitive systems to handle novelty and history. This is his primary essay’s explicit account of science’s role and changing intellectual demands, not a memoir.

readingPaths.title: The Social Function of Science
readingPaths.whyRead: Bernal directly examines the aims of science, its social responsibilities, and how methods must address novelty and history.
readingPaths.accessNote: Full primary text opened.

name: J. Georg Bednorz
institution: IBM Research Zurich, IBM Fellow Emeritus
summary: Discovered high-temperature superconductivity in copper-oxide ceramics, opening a major materials and condensed-matter research field.
activity: IBM history profile was crawled today and describes his continuing scientific legacy, IBM Fellow status, and high-temperature superconductivity; NAS profile independently documents his research and membership.
perspective: His autobiographical account traces an extended experimental search for high-temperature superconductivity and emphasizes how a close research partnership enabled risk-taking across materials and techniques.

readingPaths.title: Autobiographical account of the discovery of high-temperature superconductivity
readingPaths.whyRead: Follow the experimental sequence and the account of collaboration with Alex Müller to see how a long exploratory search was organized.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened PDF excerpt of Bednorz’s Nobel lecture autobiography, hosted by a secondary mirror; source text is his first-person Nobel lecture.

name: J. Robert Oppenheimer
summary: Theoretical physicist and director of the Los Alamos wartime laboratory; later a public voice on nuclear policy.
perspective: In a postwar essay Oppenheimer argues that open-mindedness and reasoned public engagement are necessary to govern nuclear responsibility. His approach is to resist fatalism and treat policy as a human problem requiring patient thought, rather than assume technical knowledge settles political choices.

readingPaths.title: The Open Mind
readingPaths.whyRead: Read this first-person postwar reflection on open-mindedness, public reasoning and international responsibility for atomic power.
readingPaths.accessNote: Full article accessible online.

name: Jacob Hanna
institution: Weizmann Institute of Science; Hanna Lab
summary: Breakthroughs in pluripotent stem-cell reprogramming, embryo models and ex utero mammalian development.
activity: Weizmann lab page and current team page list active PI role, current research and publications; crawled 2026-09-20.
perspective: Hanna says the rewarding part is watching trainees discover and grow; he values the freedom to pursue interesting questions without knowing where they lead, and describes uncertainty about his future research as motivating.

readingPaths.title: Member Spotlight: Jacob Hanna, MD, PhD
readingPaths.whyRead: A first-person interview with explicit reflections on what makes research exciting and how a lab develops.
readingPaths.accessNote: Accessible full text opened and read.

name: Jacques Dubochet
institution: University of Lausanne, honorary professor; Dubochet Center for Imaging
summary: Vitrification methods enabling high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy of biomolecules
activity: Dubochet Center site has 2026 facility news, events, and a substantive page on his contribution
perspective: An official Lindau report summarizes his recorded “Life as a Scientist” reflections: keep broad interests, choose long-term questions that are both interesting and feasible, accept mistakes as part of research, and share data.

readingPaths.title: Advice From Nobel Laureates: Life as a Scientist
readingPaths.whyRead: The report’s account of Dubochet’s contribution offers practical reflections on question choice, mistakes, breadth, and open science.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened Lindau Nobel Laureate Meeting annual-report PDF section summarizing a recorded event; the talk itself was not directly accessed.

name: Jacques Hadamard
summary: Proved the prime number theorem independently of de la Vallée Poussin and contributed to complex analysis, partial differential equations, and mathematical pedagogy.
perspective: Hadamard approaches mathematics through the process of invention, examining how discovery occurs rather than presenting only finished results.

readingPaths.title: The Psychology of Invention in the Mathematical Field
readingPaths.whyRead: A mathematician’s inquiry into invention and the work of mathematical discovery.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened source supports this title/description; not represented as a complete reading of the work.

name: Jahān-Malek Khātūn
summary: Injuid princess and poet whose surviving divan is described as the largest known divan by a premodern Iranian poetess; the 1995 edition contains ghazals, quatrains and other forms. Manuscript witnesses differ and exact dating of the poet’s death remains uncertain.
lifespan: Born after AH 724/1324; died after AH 784/1382–83; later death possible, not exactly established
perspective: A prose preface attributed cautiously to the poet says she composed in spare moments, initially hesitated to collect the poems because noblewomen were rarely known as poets, then compiled them after learning of earlier Arab and Persian women poets so her name would survive. This makes preservation and precedent part of her explicit literary practice.

readingPaths.title: Dīvān of Jahān Malik Khātūn, 1995 edition (Iranica discussion and bibliography)
readingPaths.whyRead: The divan’s prose preface is the strongest explicit statement of approach and intent. Iranica identifies the edition and manuscript witnesses; online primary Persian full text was not verified during this pass.
readingPaths.accessNote: Catalog/editorial route only from the opened page; full edition not accessed.

readingPaths.title: The Mirror of My Heart: A Thousand Years of Persian Poetry by Women
readingPaths.yearLabel: English translation first published 2019; publisher listing current edition
readingPaths.whyRead: A current English translation route for a selection of the poems.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened publisher description only; book text not read.

readingPaths.title: Poetic Imitation and Poetic Response
readingPaths.whyRead: Read for a careful discussion of her poetic dialogue with male contemporaries and the dangers of claiming influence too confidently.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened full article.

name: James Baldwin
summary: American novelist and essayist whose work explored race, identity and the artist’s relation to society.
perspective: Baldwin argues that an artist must actively cultivate solitude and enter a difficult, loving conflict with society. The essay treats artistic practice as a way of revealing a society to itself and making freedom possible.

readingPaths.title: The Creative Process
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the essay for Baldwin’s first-person account of solitude, artistic work and social responsibility.
readingPaths.accessNote: Full essay PDF opened; selected passages read. This direct PDF is the source for the essay; the James Baldwin Project page is corroborating context.

name: James Clerk Maxwell
summary: Unified electricity and magnetism in a field theory expressed by Maxwell’s equations, identified light as electromagnetic, and developed statistical kinetic theory of gases.
perspective: Maxwell presents theory as a disciplined cycle of selecting measurable phenomena, making explicit what the data warrant, translating between physical pictures and mathematics, and leaving unsettled questions open. He treats study of the original research record as part of learning a science.

readingPaths.title: A Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism, Vol. 1, Preface
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the preface for Maxwell’s account of selecting phenomena and using models and mathematics.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened source supports this title/description; not represented as a complete reading of the work.

name: James Gosling
institution: Amazon Web Services, Distinguished Engineer
summary: Created Java and its early compiler and runtime system, a foundational platform for globally deployed software.
activity: Personal nighthacks site resolves with current blog redirect and 2026 DNS/HTTP verification; site carries James Gosling identity and personal writing.
perspective: The Computer History Museum oral-history transcript records first-person reflections on software design values, privacy and security, usability, and the social consequences of technology.

readingPaths.title: Oral history interview with James Gosling
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the full transcript for how design choices and user experience became part of his account of making software.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened Computer History Museum archival oral-history transcript PDF.

name: James Hansen
institution: Columbia University
summary: Foundational climate modeling and early highly influential congressional testimony that brought global warming to public and policy awareness.
activity: Current role directing the Program on Climate Science Awareness and Solutions at Columbia.
perspective: Hansen says empirical evidence, especially paleoclimate data, is the principal basis for climate sensitivity estimates while models help interpret details; he also reflects on scientific communication and advocacy.

readingPaths.title: James Hansen: Taking heat for decades
readingPaths.whyRead: A substantial interview about evidence, modeling, uncertainty and public responsibility in climate science.
readingPaths.accessNote: Accessible full text opened and read.

name: James J. Heckman
institution: University of Chicago; Center for the Economics of Human Development
summary: Heckman correction and broader econometric methods for selection, plus research linking early human-capital investment to lifetime outcomes

perspective: Heckman describes learning neuroscience and child-development physiology from collaborators, following that education into new models, and valuing empirical work that understands its data and context while remaining open to criticism.

readingPaths.title: James Heckman on his early academic career and research
readingPaths.whyRead: Heckman describes learning neuroscience and child-development physiology from collaborators, following that education into new models, and valuing empirical work that understands its data and context while remaining open to criticism.

name: James Lovelock
summary: Independent scientist whose work helped formulate the Gaia hypothesis.
perspective: In his own foreword to Homage to Gaia, Lovelock connects his emotional attention to landscape with the scientist’s duty to understand Earth, and says that arrogant certainty is the antithesis of science. The source is a publisher-hosted excerpt of the memoir.

readingPaths.title: Homage to Gaia: The Life of an Independent Scientist
readingPaths.whyRead: Start with the author’s foreword, which joins his attentiveness to landscape to a scientist’s obligation to understand Earth and his caution about certainty.
readingPaths.accessNote: Publisher-hosted excerpt, not full memoir.

name: James Maynard
institution: University of Oxford; Regius Professor of Mathematics from 1 October 2026; Supernumerary Fellow of St John's College

activity: Multi-paragraph biography and research description rather than a bare listing; current roles and post-2023 FRS designation present so updated since mid-2023; corroborated by an Oxford Mathematical Institute news item of 1 July 2026 announcing his Regius Professorship
perspective: The PIMR interview presents a first-person account of research mathematics and teaching, giving an accessible entry into how he approaches proof and communicates mathematical ideas.

readingPaths.title: Interview with James Maynard
readingPaths.whyRead: A mathematician’s own account of research and teaching provides a compact entry into his style of doing and explaining mathematics.

name: James P. Allison
institution: UT MD Anderson Cancer Center
summary: CTLA-4 blockade and immune-checkpoint therapy for cancer
activity: MD Anderson profile is reachable and current as of 2026-09-20 with research and professional information
perspective: In a first-person interview Allison describes choosing a fascinating question, trusting good data, taking incremental steps, and persisting with an interesting problem.

readingPaths.title: Jim Allison interview

name: James Peebles
institution: Princeton University, Albert Einstein Professor of Science Emeritus
summary: Built the theoretical framework of modern physical cosmology, including dark matter, primordial fluctuations, and the interpretation of cosmic background radiation.

perspective: Peebles describes discomfort with weak evidence, pursuing interesting questions during a period of unusual intellectual freedom, and resisting aesthetic prejudice when observations supported an unpopular model.

readingPaths.title: Interview with James Peebles
readingPaths.whyRead: A detailed first-person account of how evidence, theory, curiosity and field structure shaped his cosmology.
readingPaths.accessNote: Accessible full text opened and read.

name: Jane Goodall
summary: Reflective writing in animal behavior and conservation.
perspective: Goodall reflects on her life and the spiritual convictions she connects with her experience studying chimpanzees. It provides a personal account of meaning and hope alongside a research life.

readingPaths.title: Reason for Hope: A Spiritual Journey
readingPaths.whyRead: A memoir of personal outlook rather than a technical account of chimpanzee research. Written with Phillip Berman.

readingPaths.whyRead: A reflective interview on research formation, methods, field change and science’s social role.

name: Jared Diamond
summary: Biogeographic and evolutionary explanations of disease, technology and state inequality; global comparative synthesis
activity: Personal site and UCLA page current; crawled 2026

readingPaths.title: How I Write: Jared Diamond

name: Jayant Narlikar

readingPaths.title: Walk the Talk with Jayant Narlikar
readingPaths.whyRead: Narlikar discusses curiosity, shared institution building and an empirical test of astrology.

name: Jayati Ghosh
institution: University of Massachusetts Amherst
summary: Development, labor, macroeconomic, and globalization research has influenced international policy debates and heterodox economics.

readingPaths.title: Interview with Jayati Ghosh
readingPaths.whyRead: A first-person account of epistemological influences, research choices and intellectual openness in political economy.

name: Jean Jennings Bartik

The reading route is a 1912 English translation, so translator and editor framing is kept distinct from the serialized Spanish original.

readingPaths.title: Filipinas dentro de Cien Años / The Philippines a Century Hence
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the essay’s conditional scenarios and compare its historical reasoning to its explicit arguments about governance and national agency.
readingPaths.accessNote: Full English translation opened; front matter and selected introduction/body passages read. Translation by Derbyshire, edited by Craig.

readingPaths.title: The Philippines a Century Hence, museum library edition note
readingPaths.whyRead: Use the edition note to separate Rizal’s serialized text from the later translator/editor and narrated/translated materials.

The speaker is fictional, so these are the work’s authored literary-philosophical ideas, not a personal confession by Gibran.

readingPaths.title: The Prophet, “On Work” and “On Teaching”
readingPaths.whyRead: These chapters set out the work’s account of meaningful craft and learner-centered teaching. Almustafa is a fictional speaker, so the work should not be treated as an autobiographical interview.
readingPaths.accessNote: Complete English-language text inspected at the author’s official website; claims are attributed to the work and its fictional speaker.

name: Kamala Sohonie
summary: Biochemist who studied the nutritive value of Indian foods and applied biochemical knowledge to nutrition and malnutrition problems.

This gives a bounded, source-mediated view of persistence, self-directed learning and adapting research to local conditions.

readingPaths.title: The Life and Times of Kamala Baghvat Sohonie

readingPaths.accessNote: The episode transcript includes selected excerpts from Sohonie’s essay, read by a voice actor, not an original recording. The original Resonance article PDF at https://www.ias.ac.in/public/Volumes/reso/021/04/0301-0314.pdf returned 403; full essay was not read.

name: Kamo no Chōmei

readingPaths.title: Hōjōki / An Account of My Hut, in Donald Keene translation
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the opening impermanence image, the disaster accounts, and the concluding hut/retreat sections as a crafted argument about attention, simplicity, and attachment.
readingPaths.accessNote: Inspected 107-page translated edition and editor’s textual note. It reports earliest 1244 copy, with postscript attributing it to Chōmei’s hand.

readingPaths.whyRead: Use for name/author and edition cross-checks.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened catalog authority page; bibliographic description, not primary text.

name: Lee Cronin
institution: University of Glasgow, Regius Professor and Chair of Chemistry; Cronin Group
summary: Introduced assembly theory and programmable complex-chemistry platforms for studying open-ended chemical complexity, artificial life, and life detection.
activity: Cronin Group page and Glasgow profile are live and show current group leadership, research themes, and recent publications.
perspective: Cronin describes curiosity-driven “blue sky” research as following a question without a predetermined end goal, allowing oneself to get lost, and iterating through divergent experiments, feedback, and simpler questions after failure. He also discusses creating an intellectually safe lab where students can explore ambitious problems.

readingPaths.title: Bye, bye, blue sky? Part 1: A conversation with Lee Cronin
readingPaths.whyRead: Podcast transcript provides direct interview responses on method, uncertainty, failure, and lab culture.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened first-person interview/oral-history text; summary grounded in the inspected passage.

name: Leo Szilard
country: Hungary / Germany / United Kingdom / United States
summary: Physicist and biophysicist whose scientific work and advocacy shaped debates on nuclear research and responsibility.
perspective: In his recollections Szilard recounts treating even a ten-percent chance of chain reaction as requiring precaution, then arguing for secrecy and publication restraint. The text shows how his judgment linked scientific uncertainty with responsibility for consequences; it is a direct reader copy of the primary recollections, checked against a university teaching guide.

readingPaths.title: Leo Szilard: His Version of the Facts: Selected Recollections and Correspondence
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the recollections alongside the included letters to see how Szilard weighed uncertainty, secrecy, and responsibility for what research might enable.
readingPaths.accessNote: Accessible reader copy opened; a university guide independently describes the book’s recollection-plus-document structure. Reader host is not the publisher.

name: Leo Tolstoy
summary: Writer whose autobiographical and religious works include A Confession.
perspective: A Confession recounts a crisis of meaning and an effort to examine his own life rather than accept inherited answers. The public text is an English translation.

readingPaths.title: A Confession
readingPaths.whyRead: A compact first-person account of a crisis of meaning and the reasoning that followed.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened the translated text index; chapter links are provided; not a full-book reading.

name: Leonardo da Vinci
summary: Renaissance artist and investigator whose notebooks record sustained studies in art, anatomy, mechanics and nature.
perspective: Leonardo’s notebooks place direct experience and observation above inherited authority. In notes on learning to paint, he advises beginning with details, proceeding step by step and cultivating diligence before speed; he also explains how to pursue the more difficult of two questions until it becomes clear. The old MacCurdy English edition is an edited translation of dispersed manuscripts, not a unified book Leonardo prepared.

readingPaths.title: The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci, selected notes on experience and learning
readingPaths.whyRead: The opening notes defend experience as evidence, while notes 491–493 give a concrete sequence for careful learning and working through difficult questions.
readingPaths.accessNote: Inspected selected passages in the MacCurdy translation via Project Gutenberg; the British Library catalog describes the manuscript and its scattered note format. The original notebooks were not read in full.

aliases: Leonardo di ser Piero da Vinci

name: Leonhard Euler
summary: Euler’s letters turn scientific and philosophical topics into sequential explanations for a young learner; the format models accessible, example-led teaching.
perspective: Euler’s letters turn scientific and philosophical topics into sequential explanations for a young learner; the format models accessible, example-led teaching.

readingPaths.title: Letters to a German Princess
readingPaths.whyRead: Euler’s letters turn scientific and philosophical topics into sequential explanations for a young learner; the format models accessible, example-led teaching.
