name: Leroy Hood
institution: Institute for Systems Biology
summary: Developing foundational instruments including the automated DNA sequencer and pioneering systems biology and P4 medicine (Predictive, Preventive, Personalized, and Participatory clinical modeling).
activity: Profile at the Institute he founded detailing current studies and his phenome project.
perspective: Hood frames leading-edge biology as dependent on inventing technologies that open new dimensions of data; he advocates an integrated loop in which biology drives technology and analytics, built by cross-disciplinary teams, and says scientists should return useful inventions to society.

readingPaths.title: Leroy Hood, MD, PhD – Life as a Scientist
readingPaths.whyRead: Hood describes these as lessons learned from building instruments and departments, not merely technical accomplishments.
readingPaths.accessNote: Accessible full interview opened and read.

name: Leslie Lamport
summary: Logical clocks, distributed-consensus theory, Paxos, and rigorous specification of concurrent systems
activity: Microsoft-maintained personal site lists publications, talks, and current materials
perspective: Lamport says he does not choose problems by timeliness; some come from engineers, others from his own ideas, and sometimes a solution suggests the problem afterward. He distinguishes real problems from artifacts of formalisms and values understanding what drives a proof, not just obtaining one.

readingPaths.title: A Discussion with Leslie Lamport
readingPaths.whyRead: Opened first-person written interview hosted by Microsoft Research.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened first-person interview/oral-history text; summary grounded in the inspected passage.

name: Leslie Valiant
institution: Harvard University, T. Jefferson Coolidge Professor
summary: Founded computational learning theory, including the PAC model, and made foundational contributions to complexity and parallel computation.
activity: Harvard profile currently links the personal research site; personal site contains CV and publications.
perspective: In a first-person interview he explains how he selected learning as a phenomenon that could be made quantitative, despite skepticism in theoretical computer science, then built a framework combining statistics and computation.

readingPaths.title: The Hunt for the Algorithms That Drive Life on Earth
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the edited Quanta interview for his own account of choosing the learning problem and turning a broad curiosity into a quantitative research program.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened primary interview or authored reflection; full book not claimed.

name: Liang Qichao
primary: Chinese intellectual, journalist, historian and reformer
topics: Chinese intellectual, journalist, historian and reformer
summary: An influential late Qing/Republic-era writer and editor who translated and commented on Western political philosophy for Chinese readers; the 1898 Politics intervention is documented by the University of Chicago study.
lifespan: 1873–1929; Politics translation and commentary composed/published in 1898, distinct from Aristotle’s ancient composition and later English scholarly translation.
perspective: In his 1898 mediation of Aristotle’s Politics, Liang selects and frames political vocabulary for a Chinese audience facing an uncertain future, using translation to argue that a new citizen concept matters politically. This is a historically situated adaptation rather than a neutral transfer of a classical text.

readingPaths.title: Liang Qichao’s 1898 translation and commentary on Aristotle’s Politics
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the source excerpt embedded in the article alongside the analysis of his framing of citizenhood and Qing political prospects.
readingPaths.accessNote: Article page and translated excerpts opened; not the complete original Chinese edition.

readingPaths.title: Liang Qichao author biography, Renditions
readingPaths.whyRead: Use the university journal’s brief biography and translations list to situate the 1898 intervention.
readingPaths.accessNote: Short author page opened; no full text access claim.

name: Linus Pauling
summary: Chemist whose work on chemical bonding and molecular structure shaped modern chemistry.
perspective: Pauling’s 1984 oral history records how he entered science, learned through cross-field conversations, and experienced institutional and public responsibilities. The transcript is first-person and explicitly marked unrestricted by Caltech; it is a life-history interview rather than a manual of technique.

readingPaths.title: Interview with Linus Pauling
readingPaths.whyRead: The oral history follows Pauling’s formation as a researcher, his interactions across fields, and his later administrative and public roles.
readingPaths.accessNote: Full Caltech transcript opened; archives state access is unrestricted.

name: Linus Torvalds
institution: Linux Foundation, Fellow
summary: Created the Linux kernel and Git, foundational systems used worldwide and models for large-scale open collaborative software development.
activity: Linux Foundation leadership page currently lists Linus Torvalds as Fellow; current Linux Foundation event and governance materials document continuing technical leadership.
perspective: TED’s page for this 2016 talk describes an interview about Torvalds’s philosophy of work, engineering, and life, and records his concise stance that he is an engineer focused on fixing the immediate practical problem. This presents a pragmatic, incremental orientation to engineering.

readingPaths.title: The mind behind Linux
readingPaths.whyRead: A conversation about his pragmatic approach to engineering, collaboration and work.
readingPaths.accessNote: TED recording page and description checked; transcript not retrieved.

name: Lisa A. Levin
institution: Scripps Institution of Oceanography, Distinguished Professor Emerita
summary: Defined deep-sea benthic ecology, methane-seep and oxygen-minimum ecosystems, and science-policy links for ocean stewardship.
activity: Personal Scripps profile and bio were crawled in the current audit; bio updated May 2026 and lists current research, publications, NAS 2024, and AGU Ocean Sciences Award 2025.
perspective: In a short self-authored professional sketch, Levin describes direct probing and sieving of marine habitats, the daily discoveries and travel that make oceanography meaningful, and the personal costs and mentoring obligations of a research career.

readingPaths.title: Sketches of Oceanographers: Lisa A. Levin
readingPaths.whyRead: Her autobiographical sketch ties field methods, curiosity, family life, and the representation of women in oceanography together.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened The Oceanography Society PDF, page 92; brief autobiographical essay, not a full memoir.

name: Lise Meitner
summary: Physicist whose research contributed to the explanation of nuclear fission.
perspective: Her retrospective Vienna talk remembers physics as a source of excitement and intellectual companionship. The open Max Planck history chapter notes how she foregrounds scientific joy and gratitude while saying little about exile, gendered institutions and personal insecurity; the limits of the narrative are part of how to read it.

readingPaths.title: “Looking Back” / “50 Jahre Physik”
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the six-page retrospective, paying attention both to what she celebrates and what she leaves outside the public account.
readingPaths.accessNote: Original talk/article is identified and substantively described in an open Max Planck history chapter; original article text not accessed.

name: Loren Eiseley
summary: Anthropologist and natural-history writer whose essays connected scientific inquiry with human experience and the natural world.
perspective: The publisher’s book description says Eiseley turns reflection and discovery toward his own life, tracing how he came to research and public renown and considering his place in society and humanity’s place in nature. This is the publisher-origin description in the book reader, not a claim that the memoir itself was read.

readingPaths.title: All the Strange Hours: The Excavation of a Life
readingPaths.whyRead: The reader preview describes the memoir as Eiseley turning his reflective powers on his own life and his place in society and nature; its contents list the self-portrait chapters.
readingPaths.accessNote: Google Books limited reader page; substantive publisher-origin description and contents are visible, not a full-text reading.

name: Lorraine Daston
institution: Max Planck Institute for the History of Science, Director Emerita
summary: Historical analysis of objectivity, probability, observation, and epistemic virtues that transformed the history of scientific knowledge and norms.
activity: MPIWG profile and archive remain active with current events/news; Max Planck reports her 2024 Balzan Prize and current recognition.
perspective: In a long interview Daston describes historical epistemology as attending to concrete scientific practices and their changing standards of rationality, rather than treating reason as timeless; she also emphasizes working across historical scales.

readingPaths.title: For a history of human rationality: an interview with Lorraine Daston
readingPaths.whyRead: A scholarly interview about the historian’s craft and the history of scientific objectivity/rationality, not simply a summary of her findings.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened primary interview or authored reflection; full book not claimed.

name: Ludwig Boltzmann
summary: Developed statistical mechanics and the kinetic theory of gases, connecting molecular motion and probability with macroscopic thermodynamic behavior.
perspective: Boltzmann treats models as extensions of thought that make complex relations graspable and communicable. They are selective analogies, useful for prediction and explanation without requiring belief that the mechanism mirrors nature literally.

readingPaths.title: “Model” (1902; reprinted in Encyclopaedia Britannica, 10th ed.; transcribed from the 1911 Britannica reprint)
readingPaths.whyRead: Read Boltzmann’s essay for how he uses models as partial aids to representing and explaining physical phenomena, not as literal copies of nature.
readingPaths.accessNote: Full text is a Wikisource transcription of the 1911 Britannica article, not a scan of the 1902 original. The contributor is abbreviated “L. Bo.”; Springer’s scholarly edition identifies “Model” as Boltzmann’s chapter and confirms its Britannica provenance.

name: Luiz Davidovich
institution: Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, emeritus
summary: Quantum optics and information research on entanglement, decoherence, quantum devices, state reconstruction, and laser theory
activity: UFRJ graduate program page lists current 2026 academic information and research areas; Brazilian Academy profile confirms academy membership and awards; audited 2026-09-20
perspective: In this Portuguese-language Pesquisa FAPESP interview, Davidovich calls science, for those involved in it, a playful activity, while also discussing scientists’ social responsibility and the institutional conditions for Brazilian science. The account presents scientific work as intrinsically engaging as well as socially situated.

readingPaths.title: Luiz Davidovich: O prazer de fazer ciência
readingPaths.whyRead: Opened Portuguese-language interview transcript; title and summary identify it as an interview about the pleasure of doing science.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened first-person interview/oral-history text; summary grounded in the inspected passage.

name: Lynn Meskell
institution: Stanford University, Professor of Anthropology and Archaeology
summary: Archaeology and heritage scholarship that made UNESCO governance, ethics, Indigenous rights, and the politics of world heritage central analytical concerns.
activity: Stanford profile has current fellowship/research information; Society for American Archaeology maintains her 2018 book-award record and Stanford reports ongoing faculty activity.
perspective: In her own explanation of A Future in Ruins, Meskell says she followed how heritage makes the past matter in the present, asking who sets political agendas and who benefits; the account foregrounds ethnographic attention to power and historical framing.

readingPaths.title: A Future in Ruins — In a nutshell
readingPaths.whyRead: Read her concise first-person framing of the questions that organized her institutional ethnography of UNESCO and World Heritage.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened author-authored book interview/editorial response; not the full book.

name: László Lovász
institution: ELTE professor emeritus; HUN-REN Alfréd Rényi Institute research professor
summary: Shaped modern combinatorics and theoretical computer science through graph theory, probabilistic methods, algorithms, and the Lovász local lemma.
activity: ELTE personal homepage is linked by current Rényi/ELTE profiles; Rényi page was updated in 2026.
perspective: Lovász describes mathematical work as alternating between trying to solve a problem and applying ideas; he prefers to clean up proofs until he understands their essential mechanism. He says one is on the wrong path much of the time, must be willing to turn back, and benefits from broad interests and publicly shared mathematics.

readingPaths.title: Interview with László Lovász
readingPaths.whyRead: Opened full open-access interview transcript in the European Mathematical Society Magazine.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened first-person interview/oral-history text; summary grounded in the inspected passage.

name: M. S. Swaminathan
summary: Agricultural scientist and institution-builder whose work joined crop science with food security and sustainable agriculture.
perspective: The publisher describes his reflections as linking life in science to people-first development, public purpose and ethical/political tensions. Chapters on criticism, managing people, research strategy and science in public policy make this an unusually direct account of how he interpreted his career.

readingPaths.title: MS Swaminathan in Conversation with Nitya Rao: From Reflections on my Life to the Ethics and Politics of Science
readingPaths.whyRead: Use Part I for life reflections and Part II for his considered discussion of politics, ethics and agricultural research.
readingPaths.accessNote: Publisher description and contents inspected; full conversation not read.

name: M. Stanley Whittingham
institution: Binghamton University, Distinguished Professor of Chemistry; NECCES director
summary: Foundational intercalation chemistry and electrode materials underlying rechargeable lithium-ion batteries.
activity: Binghamton profile accessed 2026-09-20; current titles, energy-storage research interests and contact details listed; 2026 university news confirms active battery leadership.
perspective: Whittingham distinguishes measurements on operating cells from measurements after disassembly, explaining that rested ex-situ material may differ from real operating behavior; he describes integrating theory, experiment, and operando characterization.

readingPaths.title: Stanley Whittingham Transcript
readingPaths.whyRead: Opened transcript and inspected methodological passages on operando versus ex-situ characterization. Identity/contribution named in the transcript.
readingPaths.accessNote: Full interview transcript opened. It names Whittingham and describes his work; Binghamton official profile was attempted but errored and is not used.

name: M. Visvesvaraya
summary: Civil engineer and public administrator associated with irrigation, water supply and infrastructure projects.
perspective: Visvesvaraya says he included later chapters to apply lessons from experience and observation to public life. He treats engineering as part of a wider system involving education, cooperative capacity and planned local development, and cautions that imported agencies alone cannot build a society’s capability.

readingPaths.title: Memoirs of My Working Life
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the preface and Mysore chapters for the connection he draws between engineering works, local capability and public planning.
readingPaths.accessNote: Internet Archive OCR and book record opened; the text is digitized, with OCR imperfections.

name: Magdalena Żernicka-Goetz
institution: University of Cambridge; California Institute of Technology; Zernicka-Goetz Lab
summary: Live imaging and stem-cell embryo models that reshaped understanding of mammalian cell fate, patterning and implantation.
activity: Lab site has current team and Cambridge/Caltech activity, crawled 2026-09-20; Cambridge profile lists active professor role.
perspective: Żernicka-Goetz describes curiosity about embryonic development as the driver for looking inside a previously inaccessible developmental “black box.” She says she is excited by strong ideas she does not yet know how to resolve, and advises scientists to persevere, challenge accepted thinking, and create collaborative opportunities.

readingPaths.title: An interview with Magdalena Zernicka-Goetz
readingPaths.whyRead: Opened interview transcript published in Biology of Reproduction.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened first-person interview/oral-history text; summary grounded in the inspected passage.

name: Mahmoud Darwish
summary: Palestinian poet and writer whose prose memoir connects writing, memory and civilian life during the siege of Beirut.
perspective: Darwish turns an ordinary coffee-making ritual into a practice of maintaining attention and human presence under bombardment. The passage also asks what it means to write and bear witness when ordinary life is under siege.

readingPaths.title: Memory for Forgetfulness: August, Beirut, 1982
readingPaths.yearLabel: Arabic original published 1986; English translation by Ibrahim Muhawi
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the opening coffee sequence for Darwish’s account of daily ritual, attention and writing under siege.
readingPaths.accessNote: Full English translation e-book opened and selected passages read. UC Press is the publisher, but the linked e-book itself is the direct text source; publisher product page is corroborating edition/translation context.

name: Mahmud al-Kashgari
country: Kashgar / Kara-Khanid Central Asia / Turkic-speaking regions
summary: Author of Dīwān Lughāt al-Turk, a major Arabic-facing compendium of Turkic dialects whose entries preserve lexical, grammatical, literary, ethnographic, and cartographic material. The surviving copy was made in 1266 from an authorial manuscript that is now lost.
lifespan: Active 11th century; institutional sources place composition of Dīwān Lughāt al-Turk in 1072–1074; birth/death years vary by reference and are not used here.
perspective: The work’s stated program presents Turkic vocabulary and dialects through Arabic lexicographic conventions, with examples from usage and literature and a map of Turkic peoples. Institutional descriptions say its aim included teaching Arabs Turkic and demonstrating the language’s richness; its preface also uses an explicitly pro-Turkic political register, which should be read in its 11th-century setting rather than converted into a timeless pluralist method.

readingPaths.title: Dīwān Lughāt al-Turk / Compendium of the Turkic Dialects
readingPaths.yearLabel: Composed 1072–1074; surviving manuscript copied 1266; NYU/Princeton record is a 1915–1917 Arabic edition
readingPaths.whyRead: Consult the opening preface and entries for the work’s program of presenting Turkic speech, literary examples, and lexicography to Arabic-reading audiences.
readingPaths.accessNote: The NYU Arabic Collections Online record opened and identifies the 1915–1917 Arabic edition and low-resolution scan. A separate English translation of the preface from Dankoff/Kelly was located as a 33 MB scan mirror but its PDF open failed; no direct transcription or full reading is claimed.

readingPaths.title: Dīwānü Lugâti’t-Türk, Turkish Language Association introduction
readingPaths.yearLabel: Editorial introduction by Şükrü Halûk Akalın, posted 2019
readingPaths.whyRead: Use for an overview of the collection strategy, dialects, oral literature, proverbs, map, and language-teaching purpose, while separating the author’s stated program from modern national framing.
readingPaths.accessNote: Full introduction opened, lines 2–34; it is modern institutional commentary, not the medieval text.

name: Mahzarin Banaji
institution: Harvard University; Project Implicit
summary: Development of implicit social cognition theory and the Implicit Association Test, a widely used research and public education tool.
activity: Harvard personal site and Project Implicit remain live with current CV and research resources; crawled 2026-09-20.
perspective: In an APA podcast conversation Banaji reflects on the empirical discovery and development of implicit-bias research and how people can be unaware of the influences on their judgments; the account makes the method and its limits accessible.

readingPaths.title: Can we unlearn implicit biases? With Mahzarin Banaji, PhD
readingPaths.whyRead: The transcript/podcast gives a first-person entry into why she studied implicit cognition and what the tests can and cannot tell us.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened APA podcast page with transcript/summary.

name: Mahāsī Sayādaw
summary: Burmese meditation master whose practical instructions helped make vipassanā training accessible to lay and monastic practitioners.
lifespan: 1904–1982; Manual of Insight is catalogued as 1944; English translation appeared in 2016.
perspective: Mahāsī’s instructions direct meditators to note each physical or mental event as it occurs, track arising and passing, and use direct observation to understand non-self. These are explicit instructions, not a method inferred from later practice traditions.

readingPaths.title: Practical Vipassanā Meditation Exercises
readingPaths.yearLabel: Talk/English translation by U Nyi Nyi; date not stated on opened page
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the instructions on continuous noting of bodily and mental events, their arising/passing, and insight into non-self.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened the full online instructional text and inspected those sections; translated by U Nyi Nyi.

readingPaths.title: Manual of Insight
readingPaths.whyRead: Use the book’s practical exposition alongside the exercise instructions.
readingPaths.accessNote: Publisher page identifies author, dates, book, and translation; full book not opened.

name: Maimonides
country: al-Andalus / North Africa / Egypt / Jewish intellectual history
summary: Maimonides wrote the Guide of the Perplexed in Judeo-Arabic in the 12th century, engaging the problems of biblical interpretation, philosophy and religious learning. The Guide became a major work in Jewish thought and circulated through Hebrew translations.
lifespan: 1135–1204 according to Friedländer’s biographical introduction in the open 1904 edition; the source is a 19th-century scholarly biography
perspective: Maimonides tells a philosophically trained reader to investigate apparent contradictions and figurative language rather than assume every scriptural passage is literal. The book’s introduction combines lexical analysis, attention to reader preparation, and an intentionally structured presentation of difficult ideas; Friedländer’s older English edition also points to Maimonides’ rule to believe what is graspable by reason, sense, or trustworthy authority.

readingPaths.title: Mishneh Torah, Introduction and Preface
readingPaths.whyRead: The introduction sets out why he undertook the work, how he organized the material and how he intended the result to make legal knowledge accessible.
readingPaths.accessNote: Inspected the Mechon Mamre English translation, reconstructed according to Yemenite manuscripts, and used the Stanford Encyclopedia for independent identity and reception context.

readingPaths.title: The Guide for the Perplexed, trans. M. Friedländer
readingPaths.yearLabel: Judeo-Arabic composition in the late 12th century; English translation 1881/1904
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the author’s prefatory remarks and “Directions for the Study of this Work,” then sample Part I’s treatment of equivocal biblical language.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened public PDF; selected introduction and contents, not entire work. This is an older translation; Chicago Press describes Shlomo Pines’s later translation as a standard reader route.

readingPaths.title: The Guide of the Perplexed, trans. Shlomo Pines
readingPaths.whyRead: Use the later scholarly translation with Leo Strauss’s introduction; publisher page notes its purpose is to address readers’ literal interpretation difficulties.
readingPaths.accessNote: Publisher page opened; book access through purchase or library, not read in this pass.

name: Manjul Bhargava
institution: Princeton University; Robert C. Gunning and R. Brandon Fradd Professor in Mathematics
summary: Discovered higher composition laws generalising Gauss composition; then used a new geometry-of-numbers method to count rings and fields of small rank and to bound the average rank of elliptic curves; effectively founding modern arithmetic statistics
activity: Profile lists 58 research outputs with 2025 and 2026 items including work on Galois groups of random integer polynomials and a 2026 item on rank stability in quadratic extensions; records an active NSF grant running through 2028
perspective: In a full interview transcript Bhargava discusses how music and Sanskrit patterns shaped his mathematical imagination and how he sees mathematics as creative, accessible work rather than only formal technique.

readingPaths.title: India Questions Math Genius Professor Manjul Bhargava: Full Transcript
readingPaths.whyRead: Read for his account of the cultural and musical materials he carries into mathematics and the way he thinks about communicating it.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened full interview transcript; source is a news interview, not an academic archive.

name: Manūščihr ī Juwān-jam
summary: Ninth-century Zoroastrian high priest and author of the Pahlavi question-and-answer work called Dādestān ī Dēnīg; he described it as a book of questions and answered community queries on religious, ethical, social, legal, philosophical and cosmological matters.
lifespan: Ninth century CE; the only explicit life-date in the opened scholarly source is completion of another work in 881 CE.
perspective: In his introduction Manūščihr says he gathers remembered teaching from earlier authorities, recognizes that predecessors disagree, and adopts the judgment that seems most reasonable while acknowledging alternatives. His replies model tradition-based adjudication that includes explicit reasoning about conflicting authorities.

readingPaths.title: Dādestān ī Dēnīg (Religious Judgements), selected questions and answers
readingPaths.yearLabel: 9th c. composition; the opening packet’s manuscripts/text history require a critical edition; SOAS thesis covers chapters 1–35
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the introduction and selected question-answer cases to see how inherited doctrine and practical reasoning are brought together.
readingPaths.accessNote: SOAS repository search result identifies a transcription/translation/commentary thesis (chapters 1–35), but the PDF viewer returned an internal error. Another translated chapters 1–41 path is listed at Avesta.org, but its page also returned an internal error. Treat this as a concrete library/repository route, not as text inspected.

name: Marcus Aurelius
summary: Reflective writing in practical philosophy.
perspective: Marcus begins by naming particular habits he learned from particular people: careful reading, correction without humiliation, simplicity and steadiness. The account makes character a matter of remembered examples and repeated practice.

readingPaths.title: Meditations — Book One
readingPaths.yearLabel: Second century CE; George Long translation
readingPaths.whyRead: Book One is a compact record of influences and habits, before the later books’ exercises in self-examination.
readingPaths.accessNote: Translated text hosted by MIT; Book One inspected.

name: Margaret Hamilton
summary: Software engineer who led the Apollo flight-software effort and helped establish software engineering as a discipline.
lifespan: Exact dates not verified in this source pass.
perspective: The interview segments and Hamilton’s remarks reproduced by MIT/NASA emphasize abstract thinking, learning from failures, priorities, and the responsibility of taking software seriously. Her recollection frames problem solving as a collaborative process with no second chance, rather than a lone act of coding.

readingPaths.title: Margaret Hamilton in Her Own Words — CHM oral-history selections
readingPaths.whyRead: The clip index directs readers to Hamilton discussing abstract thinking, software errors, programming priorities, and how she solves problems.
readingPaths.accessNote: CHM page describes and embeds selected clips and links to the full transcript/video. I inspected the page and its editorial descriptions; the transcript link returned an error during this review, and I did not claim to have watched the clips.

name: Margaret Lucas Cavendish, Duchess of Newcastle
summary: Seventeenth-century philosopher and writer whose published works include Observations Upon Experimental Philosophy, Philosophical Letters and The Blazing World; SEP situates her arguments within debates about knowledge, sense, matter and authority.
lifespan: 1623–1673 (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy).
perspective: Cavendish challenges confidence in instruments and experimental reports by stressing limits of sense perception and the need to distinguish observation from interpretation; she explores alternative causal accounts and uses dialogue/fiction to test how observers and communities shape knowledge. Her philosophical stance also examines how reception affects whether a person can count as an authoritative investigator.

readingPaths.title: Observations Upon Experimental Philosophy, with The Description of a New Blazing World
readingPaths.yearLabel: 1666 first edition; this digitized second edition appeared 1668
readingPaths.whyRead: Compare her critique of microscope-based claims in Observations with the fictional disputations in Blazing World.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened the digitized 1668 edition’s title/metadata and selected-page index; not all pages were inspected. SEP scholarly synthesis supplies the approach; the work is also available in modern critical editions.

name: Margaret Mead
country: United States / Samoa / Papua New Guinea
summary: Anthropologist whose ethnographic and public work shaped twentieth-century cultural anthropology.
perspective: The book’s own reader description identifies Blackberry Winter as Mead’s autobiography and describes her life as a woman and anthropologist, explicitly linking scholarship with concern for ordinary people. This entry relies on that descriptive account of her own work, not a close reading of the full memoir.

readingPaths.title: Blackberry Winter: My Earlier Years
readingPaths.whyRead: Mead’s autobiography recounts her life as a woman and anthropologist and frames scholarship in relation to ordinary people.
readingPaths.accessNote: Google Books reader/catalog record opened; full memoir not inspected.

name: Maria Cunitz
country: Silesia / Oleśnica / Oels / Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth / Holy Roman Empire
summary: Published Urania propitia (1650), a two-part Latin and German work of astronomical tables based on Kepler’s Rudolphine Tables; her husband’s preface explicitly disclaimed authorship.
lifespan: Born c. 1604–1610; died 22 or 24 August 1664 (birth and day of death differ among scholarly references).
perspective: Cunitz adapted Keplerian tables and reorganized calculations to make planetary positions easier to compute; the scholarly biography also records contemporary criticism that convenience could come at a cost in accuracy. Her choice to provide explanatory German alongside Latin made the work usable beyond Latin-trained readers, according to the title, catalog records and scholarly biography.

readingPaths.title: Urania propitia sive tabulae astronomicae mirè faciles
readingPaths.whyRead: Use the Latin and German parts to compare Cunitz’s exposition and tables with the Keplerian framework; inspect the preface and instructions alongside the tables to see how she translates theory into a practical calculation procedure.
readingPaths.accessNote: Google Books record offers full-view controls, and Indiana University provides a physical-library catalog record; this pass inspected bibliographic metadata only, not the book’s pages. The Wielkopolska digital-library object has a public-domain record but its page images were gated by CAPTCHA.

name: Marie Curie

Her argument treats education as practical preparation for ethical independence and citizenship, not as ornamental accomplishment.

readingPaths.title: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
readingPaths.whyRead: Start with the chapters on human duties, prevailing assumptions about sexual difference, and the causes of women’s social degradation.

name: Mau Piailug

readingPaths.title: Neil Turok oral history interview
readingPaths.whyRead: First-person oral-history transcript on research setbacks, problem choice, and transition into a more self-directed environment.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened page; summary limited to the inspected first-person text/interview description.

name: Nguyễn Trãi
summary: Quốc âm thi tập is a 254-poem Nôm collection associated with Nguyễn Trãi and central to the history of vernacular Vietnamese writing; the collection survives through later manuscript/print transmission, not as a securely dated autograph in this record.
lifespan: 1380–1442; one opened foundation page links to an unreviewed biographical source, while institutional literature sources establish his role; poem collection is 14th–15th c. and manuscript/printing witnesses postdate composition.
perspective: The collection’s language repays word-level, context-sensitive reading: a university study compares each occurrence of an old Nôm word with earlier annotations and argues for semantic/pragmatic revisions. This supports an interpretive practice of reading local usage against received glosses, not a claim that we know his private method.

readingPaths.title: Quốc âm thi tập (Collected Poems in the National Language)
readingPaths.yearLabel: 14th–15th c. collection; specific composition dates uncertain
readingPaths.whyRead: Read poems alongside the Nôm characters, dictionary, literary allusion index, and translations; compare lexical choices against scholarly annotations.
readingPaths.accessNote: Foundation introduction and poem-navigation/dictionary access opened; full 254 poems not read in this task.

readingPaths.whyRead: Use the specialist chapter as a scholarly orientation to the poem collection; chapter text is authentication-gated.

name: Ngô Bảo Châu
institution: University of Chicago, Francis and Rose Yuen Distinguished Service Professor
summary: Proved the fundamental lemma through new algebro-geometric methods, a central advance in the Langlands program.
activity: UChicago profile is current and explicitly links his personal site; personal page contains research papers and preprints though last crawl is older.
perspective: Châu describes learning mathematics by trying hard problems, then carefully copying and understanding a solution until he can transfer its idea to a new problem; he values deep comprehension over problem counts.

readingPaths.title: Ngô Bảo Châu on the problem he spent an afternoon unable to solve
readingPaths.whyRead: The opened Vietnamese Q&A gives a precise first-person learning practice and explains how difficulty and an elegant solution deepened his interest.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened the full Vietnamese-language interview. The entry description is a careful translation/paraphrase of the source, not a direct quotation.

name: Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o
summary: Kenyan novelist, playwright and essayist whose writing examined language, colonial power and cultural knowledge.
perspective: Ngũgĩ argues that languages are repositories of situated knowledge and that translation should enable mutual exchange rather than a one-way hierarchy. readingPaths.title: Reclaiming Language: A Conversation With Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the author’s answers on language, knowledge, translation and literary form.
readingPaths.accessNote: The Nation interview page opened; selected answers read. Its date is June 2, 2025, shortly before Ngũgĩ’s death, and it notes editing for length. The 2018 Scroll interview is corroborating, not the source for this entry.

name: Niels Bohr
summary: Introduced a quantized model of the atom in 1913 that accounted for hydrogen spectral lines and shaped early quantum theory.
perspective: In the transcribed lecture Bohr uses the problem of observing living systems to examine how an investigative method can shape what counts as an adequate account. The 2025 article supplies the earliest English version and editorial context; the lecture itself is Bohr’s 1932 work.

readingPaths.title: ‘Light and Life’ (1932 lecture; earliest-English-version transcription in ‘A Return to Niels Bohr’s “Light and Life” (1932)’)
readingPaths.whyRead: Bohr’s address explores how the conditions of observation and concepts from physics bear on biological inquiry, exposing his cross-disciplinary way of reasoning.
readingPaths.accessNote: The opened Springer article includes a transcription of the lecture’s earliest English version, introduced by a 2025 scholarly essay. It is a transcription from an archival pamphlet, not a scan of Bohr’s manuscript; the publisher page may have access restrictions outside the visible abstract/transcription.

name: Nikki Keddie
institution: University of California, Los Angeles, professor emerita
summary: Established influential comparative and social histories of modern Iran, Islam, secularism, revolution, and women’s history.
activity: Personal site remains reachable with biography and scholarly autobiography; UCLA profile was refreshed in 2026 and confirms emerita status.
perspective: Keddie reflects that oral-history interviewees offered beliefs and interpretations rather than simply recorded facts, and describes how a global, multilingual preparation shaped her historical lens.

readingPaths.title: Nikki Keddie: Biography and reflections on oral history
readingPaths.whyRead: Her self-authored account makes research method explicit, especially the interpretive limits of oral testimony and the role of preparation in framing questions.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened the linked first-person source; this describes the material inspected, not an entire book or recording.

name: Niko Tinbergen
summary: Reflective writing in animal behavior.
perspective: Tinbergen describes how watching animals in their own surroundings produces questions and experiments. His field accounts make the patience, conditions and inventive small tests behind a discovery visible.

readingPaths.accessNote: Publisher description and contents checked; full book not reviewed. Library or purchase may be needed.

He explains that he pursued a controversial account after weighing criticism and the risk of misunderstanding, because he believed it approached the truth.

readingPaths.title: My Days with Gandhi: author’s preface

He explains that he pursued a controversial account after weighing criticism and the risk of misunderstanding, because he believed it approached the truth.
readingPaths.accessNote: The book’s title page and preface were inspected in an online OCR mirror. Access is to a reproduced scan/transcription, not a critical edition; use this limited access note.

name: Nise da Silveira
summary: Brazilian psychiatrist whose practice rejected coercive treatment and used creative activity in psychiatric care.

readingPaths.title: Interview on Cartas a Spinoza and occupational therapy
readingPaths.whyRead: Read Silveira’s answers about her encounter with Spinoza, her departure from coercive treatment and her use of art as therapy.
readingPaths.accessNote: Portuguese Folha de S.Paulo interview page opened; selected direct answers read. UNESCO archive page is corroborating identity/archive provenance, not the interview source.

name: Norbert Wiener
summary: Founded cybernetics as a cross-disciplinary study of communication and control and made foundational contributions to stochastic processes, harmonic analysis, and prediction.

readingPaths.title: I Am a Mathematician
readingPaths.whyRead: An autobiographical continuation of Wiener’s account of mathematical and scientific life; publisher page gives bibliographic context.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened source supports this title/description; not represented as a complete reading of the work.

name: Norman Foster
institution: Norman Foster Foundation, President; Foster + Partners, Founder and Executive Chairman
summary: Shaped high-technology architecture and urban design through a sustained body of work, writing, teaching, archival research, and foundation-led research on cities, infrastructure, and sustainable design.
activity: Foundation news and research pages show 2026 programmes, publications, archives, debates, and the Norman Foster Institute.
perspective: Foster describes an architectural practice in which roughly 150 professions work together from the start; he frames integration and systems thinking as the means to make buildings do more with less. He also recounts research into concrete finishes that could withstand and be cleaned of graffiti.

readingPaths.title: Norman Foster: “En vivienda se ha desplazado todo de lo público a lo privado, hay que encontrar un mejor equilibrio”
readingPaths.whyRead: Spanish-language interview explaining early interdisciplinary integration and systems thinking in architectural practice, with a concrete material-research example.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened page; summary limited to the inspected first-person text/interview description.

name: Nāgārjuna
summary: Second-century Buddhist philosopher associated with the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā and Vigrahavyāvartanī.
lifespan: c. 150–250 CE; Stanford notes scant biography and legendary accounts
perspective: The Vigrahavyāvartanī stages objections in question-and-answer form and answers them through arguments about emptiness, knowledge, names and language. The work offers a reader a model of exposing a claim to objections and clarifying what its terms can establish.

readingPaths.title: The Dispeller of Disputes: Nāgārjuna’s Vigrahavyāvartanī
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the OUP translation with its introduction and commentary; it gives the text’s question-and-answer structure and addresses authenticity and epistemology.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened OUP scholarly description, which documents the translation, text history and commentary; the entire book was not read.

name: Octavia E. Butler
summary: A science-fiction writer whose autobiographical essays describe how she built and sustained a writing practice.
perspective: Butler presents persistence as a craft habit: aim deliberately, keep writing through doubt and rejection, and learn the practical mechanics of submitting work. She does not reduce the process to confidence; she describes fear, economic pressure and long stretches without sales.

readingPaths.title: Positive Obsession
readingPaths.whyRead: Read Butler’s autobiographical account of how a chosen goal and steady work survived fear, rejection and limited opportunity.
readingPaths.accessNote: Library of America text opened; relevant passages about aim, doubt, writing hours and rejection were read.

name: Okot p’Bitek
summary: Ugandan poet and anthropologist, author of Wer pa Lawino / Song of Lawino and related self-translated poetic novels.
lifespan: 1931–1982; birth/death day differs across library sources, so only years are used here
perspective: In Song of Lawino, p’Bitek uses a culturally situated first-person voice to stage conflict over changing Acholi life. A Gale reference account describes his combination of Acholi oral traditions and contemporary political themes, while a peer-reviewed article traces the poem’s relation to Acoli song forms and songs he collected.

readingPaths.title: Wer pa Lawino / Song of Lawino
readingPaths.yearLabel: Song of Lawino first published in English in 1966 in p’Bitek’s own translation; full Acholi-language publication date varies across bibliographic records (1966/1969); reprint in 1984 combined edition
readingPaths.whyRead: Read the Acholi original alongside p’Bitek’s own English translation where available; focus on the dramatic voice and cultural metaphors rather than treating the English version as a neutral mirror.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened bibliographic page, table of contents and author biography with limited preview controls; full poem not read. BnF authority record independently confirms author, dates/years, Acholi writing and poet status. Peer-reviewed Postcolonial Text article supports oral-song relationship; its linked PDF is available from the page but was not opened.

name: Olaudah Equiano
country: Igboland / claimed Essaka, present-day Nigeria (birthplace disputed) / Atlantic world / Britain
summary: Author and public advocate whose 1789 Interesting Narrative recounts enslavement, maritime experience, conversion, freedom and abolitionist politics.
lifespan: 1745–1797 as used in Oxford and Project Gutenberg authority metadata; birthplace disputed in recent scholarship (Equiano says Essaka in Igboland; Carretta argues South Carolina).
perspective: Equiano frames life writing as both a claim to the right of Black self-authorship and a persuasive account for an audience largely unfamiliar with slavery; the narrative links remembered experience to religious reflection and abolitionist argument. Scholarship treats its first-person account as a crafted rhetorical project and cautions that its claimed African birthplace is disputed, without erasing the text’s historical and literary value.

readingPaths.title: The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, or Gustavus Vassa, the African
readingPaths.yearLabel: First published 1789; Project Gutenberg provides the 1789 text
readingPaths.whyRead: Read Chapter I’s account of the author’s country and customs, then Chapter X for the narrative’s explicit process of reading, reflection and conversion. Track how the autobiography addresses the reader and binds personal experience to the abolitionist case.
readingPaths.accessNote: Opened the complete public-domain HTML text and inspected the title/front matter and selected passages including Chapter X; did not read the whole narrative. Oxford’s editorial discussion flags the disputed birthplace and 1789 abolitionist context.

readingPaths.title: Manifesto Antropófago / Cannibalist Manifesto

readingPaths.whyRead: Read the manifesto alongside its scholarly introduction for a method of transforming outside influences rather than copying them.

name: P. C. Mahalanobis
summary: Indian statistician who founded the Indian Statistical Institute and advanced sample-survey methods and statistical planning.

He explains that representative random sampling helps avoid bias, while conclusions remain uncertain and their uncertainty can itself be estimated.

readingPaths.whyRead: In his presidential address, Mahalanobis argues that variation is intrinsic across physical, biological, and social measurements; useful inference must take it into account. He explains that representative random sampling helps avoid bias, while conclusions remain uncertain and their uncertainty can itself be estimated.

name: R. K. Narayan

name: Richard Hamming
summary: Hamming made foundational contributions to error-detecting and error-correcting codes, numerical methods, and digital filtering. perspective: Across the course and the 1986 Bellcore talk, Hamming treats strong scientific work as a learnable practice: clarify and choose consequential problems, cultivate habits and working conditions that support original thought, and examine how reasoning actually unfolded in concrete cases. His teaching joins technical examples with analysis of the decisions and thought processes behind them, rather than presenting discovery as a list of results.

summary: Discovered powerful climate forcing by CFCs and non-CO2 pollutants and built science-policy responses to short-lived climate pollutants.
